answer.label: Attributed to

answer.sourceLine: Widely credited to Mother Teresa and squarely in line with what she taught and how she wrote. But the entire citation trail runs through a single uncited line on Wikiquote — “as quoted in Mother Teresa: Come Be My Light (2007)” — with no page given, and the only scan of that book we could reach is lending-restricted, so we could not open it and confirm the sentence.

trail: Wikiquote’s Mother Teresa page ↗ carries the line in its sourced section, credited “As quoted in Mother Teresa: Come Be My Light (2007) by Brian Kolodiejchuk” — and its Misattributed section, which flags the Paradoxical Commandments, does not mention this line at all.

The book is real and checkable: the 2007 Doubleday first edition, edited by Brian Kolodiejchuk, is catalogued at the Internet Archive ↗. The scan is access-restricted, so we could not search it for the sentence, and no page number appears in any secondary citation.
Every quote site we opened copies the same line without adding anything. QuotePark says so outright ↗ — “Adopted from Wikiquote” — and Lib Quotes ↗ reproduces the identical citation with no page.

Quote Investigator has never examined this sentence: its Mother Teresa category ↗ holds one article, on the Paradoxical Commandments. With no specialist finding to lean on and no page to check, attributed is as far as the evidence goes.
source.excerptNote: The ellipsis is not ours. Wikiquote prints the line with four dots between the halves — a full stop plus an ellipsis — which conventionally marks omitted material, meaning the two sentences may not have been adjacent in the original. Whatever stood between them is not reproduced anywhere we could reach.
source.rightsHolder: The estate of Mother Teresa / the Missionaries of Charity, and Doubleday, New York (2007 edition)
source.rightsNote: The work this line is cited to, Mother Teresa: Come Be My Light, was first published by Doubleday in 2007 — a decade after her death — so it is firmly under United States copyright. Her underlying letters and instructions, published or not, remain with her estate; there is no public-domain edition of this text, and no earlier published source for the wording has been identified.

author.name: Mother Teresa
author.heading: About Mother Teresa
author.metaLine: 1910–1997 · Catholic nun & founder of the Missionaries of Charity
author.bio: Born Anjezë Gonxhe Bojaxhiu in Skopje on 26 August 1910, she founded the Missionaries of Charity in Calcutta in 1950 and spent nearly half a century running homes for the dying, the abandoned and the sick. She received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1979, died on 5 September 1997, and was canonised by the Catholic Church on 4 September 2016. Her characteristic teaching was exactly this one — that scale is the wrong measure of a good act — which is why so many differently-worded versions of it circulate under her name.

misattribution.heading: The wording problem
misattribution.intro: Nothing here says Mother Teresa didn’t say it. The trouble is that this thought travels in half a dozen shapes under her name, and the shape most people share is not the one with a citation attached to it.

items.who: “Not all of us can do great things. But we can do small things with great love.”
items.why: This, not the wording on this page, is what actually circulates. Goodreads shows it with 22,716 likes, no book source of any kind, and reader tags reading ‘misattributed-to-mother-teresa’ and ‘paraphrased’ ↗.

items.who: “In this life we cannot do great things…” / “We can’t all do great things…”
items.why: The Society of the Little Flower prints “In this life we cannot do great things. We can only do small things with great love” ↗ under her name, while another retelling calls “We can’t all do great things, but we can do little things with great love” her famous quote ↗. Small or little, cannot or can’t — there is no fixed text.

The sentiment is Thérèse’s “Little Way,” and the overlap is not a coincidence: Mother Teresa chose the name “Teresa” because she was inspired by St. Therese of Lisieux’s capability to do ordinary things with extraordinary love ↗. Two saints, one idea, endlessly swapped credit.

items.who: Mother Teresa as a quote magnet
items.why: Her single most-shared “quote” is not hers. Quote Investigator traces the “Do it anyway” Paradoxical Commandments to Kent M. Keith, who wrote them as a Harvard student in 1968 ↗; the credit drifted to her after a 1995 book showed them posted on a wall at one of her children’s homes.

misattribution.truthLine: The idea is unmistakably hers. The sentence rests on one uncited entry in Wikiquote’s sourced list ↗, which names the posthumous Come Be My Light (2007) and gives no page — so we call it attributed, not verified.

context.heading: Why this one is hard to pin down
lead: Mother Teresa said some version of this constantly. That is the problem. The thought — that the size of an act is the wrong thing to measure, and that a smaller act demands more love rather than less — runs through her talks, letters and instructions for decades, and it comes back out in a dozen different sentences. Some are hers word for word; some are a listener’s summary that hardened into a quotation.

There is also a small typographic tell. Wikiquote prints the line as “great love....The smaller the thing” — four dots, a full stop plus an ellipsis, which conventionally marks material left out between two sentences. Read literally, the two halves everyone shares as one quotation may not have stood next to each other in whatever Mother Teresa originally wrote. Nothing we could find reproduces the omitted middle, and the one book cited is not searchable online.
detailsBody: We checked her most-quoted set-piece text, the address to the National Prayer Breakfast of 3 February 1994 ↗. It does not contain this line; its nearest relative is “It is not how much we do, but how much love we put into what we do.”
Quote Investigator, the usual court of last resort, has not investigated this sentence. Its Mother Teresa file ↗ holds a single article, and it is about a text that turned out not to be hers at all.
We could not search the cited book. The 2007 Doubleday first edition is catalogued at the Internet Archive ↗, but the scan is access-restricted, so its full text is closed to search.
context.pull: The idea is unmistakably hers. The sentence is a citation with no page behind it.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote's sourced section lists "Don't look for big things, just do small things with great love....The smaller the thing, the greater must be our love." credited only as "As quoted in Mother Teresa: Come Be My Light (2007) by Brian Kolodiejchuk", with no page; its Misattributed section contains only the Paradoxical Commandments.

The Internet Archive item page confirms Mother Teresa: Come Be My Light: The Private Writings of the "Saint of Calcutta", edited by Brian Kolodiejchuk, published by Doubleday, New York, 2007; the scan is access-restricted.

Quote Investigator concludes Kent M. Keith crafted the Paradoxical Commandments as a Harvard student in 1968, that they were misattributed to at least four people including Mother Teresa, and that the Mother Teresa credit stems from the 1995 book A Simple Path showing them posted on a wall at one of her children's homes.
Quote Investigator's Mother Teresa category lists only the Paradoxical Commandments article — there is no QI investigation of "small things with great love".

Goodreads shows "Not all of us can do great things. But we can do small things with great love." credited to Mother Teresa with 22,716 likes, no book source, tagged 'misattributed-to-mother-teresa' and 'paraphrased'.

The Society of the Little Flower states Mother Teresa chose the name 'Teresa' because she was inspired by St. Therese of Lisieux's capability to do ordinary things with extraordinary love, and prints "In this life we cannot do great things. We can only do small things with great love." credited to Mother Teresa.
This page calls "We can't all do great things, but we can do little things with great love" Mother Teresa's famous quote and links the idea to Thérèse of Lisieux.
QuotePark gives the identical citation "As quoted in Mother Teresa: Come Be My Light (2007) by Brian Kolodiejchuk" and states the entry was "Adopted from Wikiquote".
Lib Quotes reproduces the quote with the citation "As quoted in Mother Teresa: Come Be My Light (2007) by Brian Kolodiejchuk" and gives no page number, chapter or date.

Mother Teresa was born Anjezë Gonxhe Bojaxhiu on 26 August 1910 in Skopje, died 5 September 1997, founded the Missionaries of Charity in 1950, received the 1979 Nobel Peace Prize and was canonised on 4 September 2016.

Mother Teresa's address at the National Prayer Breakfast of 3 February 1994 does not contain the "small things with great love" line; its nearest wording is "It is not how much we do, but how much love we put into what we do."
